stories.title: Malawi: 9 in 10 Malawians Shut Out of Bank Loans Because They Work in 'Shadow Economy' - Economist
stories.summary: Malawi: 9 in 10 Malawians Shut Out of Bank Loans Because They Work in 'Shadow Economy' - Economist The Guardian 7 September 2026 Nyasa Times (Leeds) Millions of hardworking Malawians and small business owners are being frozen out of formal bank loans simply because of HOW they earn their living, a leading economist has warned. Dr Bertha Bangala Chikadza, President of the Economic Association of Malawi (ECAMA) and a senior macroeconomics lecturer at the University of Malawi, revealed that an eye-watering 92.6 percent of the country's population works in the informal sector -- making it virtually impossible for banks to verify their income or work out how risky they are to lend to. "Formal credit remains difficult for many Malawians to access largely because 92.6 percent of the population is employed in the informal sector," she said, citing figures from the International Labour Organisation. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) are suffering the same fate, Chikadza warned, as many operate without the financial paperwork or assets that lenders demand. She said sky-high interest rates were making things even worse -- piling extra costs onto borrowing and scaring small businesses away from taking out loans to invest and grow. "Usually, loans taken for investment purposes take long to materialise, leaving borrowers exposed to repayment obligations before the investments start generating income," she explained. And it doesn't stop there -- Chikadza said strict collateral rules are shutting out people and households who could easily afford to repay a loan, but simply don't have enough assets to put up as security.

stories.summary: Africa: Climate, Clean-Air Action Could Return $15 for Every $1 Invested - UN 7 September 2026 Capital FM (Nairobi) By Bruhan Makong Nairobi — Every US$1 invested in tackling climate change and air pollution together could generate about US$15 in economic benefits, a new United Nations assessment has found, strengthening the case for governments and investors to treat environmental action as an economic investment rather than a cost. The report by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) warns that failure to act is already carrying a huge economic price, with each year of delayed action estimated to forgo more than US$1.5 trillion in benefits, equivalent to about 0.5 per cent of global GDP. The findings are contained in Hidden Assets: The Economic and Health Case for Climate and Clean Air Action , released on Monday to coincide with the International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies. It is described as the first comprehensive global economic assessment of integrated climate and clean-air action. The report found that combining climate and air-pollution policies generates significantly greater returns than addressing the two challenges separately, because many of the same sources and sectors drive both problems.

Many of the women have not previously worked in Sudan , where conservative social norms dictate that men are usually responsible for financial support. Without established trades or professions, and with their husbands and other family members dead or missing, many female refugees are struggling to pay for food, medical care and rent. The Guardian spoke to 19 aid workers, refugees and medical professionals who say a lack of access to healthcare, education and, at times, food has made the situation for Sudanese women in Egypt increasingly desperate. stories.title: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'
stories.summary: Image caption, David Etor's first break came after designing and building a kind of "solar oven" in Nigeria By James Diamond ,Â Bristol Â and Â John Darvall ,Â BBC Radio Bristol Published 7 September 2026 A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field. David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in the School of Electrical, Electronic and Mechanical Engineering at the University of Bristol. He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our dignity" in front of neighbours. "I didn't see a way out," he said. 'The poor called us poor' Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his memoir, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom. "It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said. "I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water. "[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food... "She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water. "She was trying to protect our dignity." stories.title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

The "Correct the Map" resolution adopted by the General Assembly aims to fix the discrepancy with the Mercator map, in which the African continent is shown as being of similar size to Greenland - even though it is in reality about 14 times larger. The UN adopted a new map, the Equal Earth projection, which better represents the true sizes of landmasses - but comes with problems of its own. There have been many prominent attempts over the years to solve the problem of accurately representing the surface of a sphere on a flat rectangle, each with its own benefits and drawbacks. stories.title: Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The embrace of Russia by Niger, and other Sahel states, has been seen as a rejection of the post-colonial Western powers By Simi Jolaoso Africa correspondent Published 5 September 2026 When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia. Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport. Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger. Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny". "This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule." The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.

In what became known as the Sharpeville massacre, police infamously opened fire on thousands of peaceful demonstrators. A bullet is still lodged in Mofokeng's spine, and he has a gentle limp from a gunshot to the leg. "We weren't seen as people," the 86-year-old tells the BBC as he explains the reasons he joined the demonstration on 21 March 1960 against the repressive laws of the white-minority government. "All you were good for was working. You couldn't question them, you were supposed to just do as you're told." The massacre at Sharpeville, which he survived, exposed to the world the violence of the racist apartheid system - yet thanks to an indemnity law passed a year after the killings, none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted. Mofokeng is now part of a legal case announced on Thursday that will seek to overturn this law.

Photograph: Courtesy of CCF Bring on the drones: how a technology revolution is being rolled out across Africa’s nature reserves As graduates of an online training course gather from across the continent, the consensus is overwhelming: computers and saving animals go together O n a bitingly cold night in Lapalala Wilderness nature reserve in South Africa’s Limpopo province, Duncan Kanyakera watches as instructor Jacques Viljoen deploys a thermal drone in search of a lone cheetah. Many of the students – from 11 African countries as far flung as Benin, Liberia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar – witnessing the demonstration have earned their places at Lapalala after performing well on an online training programme for protected area technicians (PAT) run by the Connected Conservation Foundation (CCF).

stories.title: 'The crowd shouted that we'd stolen someone's genitals' - deadly rumours spread on social media
stories.summary: Image source, Alfred Lasteck / BBC Image caption, Boniface Mgala and a friend were pulled out of a restaurant and attacked by a mob that accused them of stealing a man's genitals By Mungai Ngige ,Â BBC Global Disinformation Unit Â and Â Alfred Lasteck ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Tunduma Published 3 September 2026 More than 80 people were killed between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries. The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media. "They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief. His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen. Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread.

Photograph: Alamy Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found. Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network , found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year. Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year.

stories.title: Women behind the lens: ‘The women are moving towards the church, but it is not the final destination’

View image in fullscreen In her work entitled Holy Gang, artist Puleng Mongale says ‘the sun represents a place where I can meet my ancestors beyond religious limitations’. Women behind the lens: ‘The women are moving towards the church, but it is not the final destination’ South African artist Puleng Mongale explores how her childhood church still connects her to the women of her family, not through religion but shared history and memory T his image, called Holy Gang, combines an image of a church in my mother’s home town, Fateng-tse-Ntsho, in Free State province, South Africa , with self-portraits of me, multiplied to form a group of women. Although at first glance the women are moving towards the church, it is not the final destination. Positioned higher, beyond the church, is what appears to be a rising sun.
